name: Latin (Classical, active method)
ttsNote: There is no Latin voice on iPhone. Audio uses the Italian voice with Latin respelled toward Classical sounds (hard c and g, v → w, ae → 'eye'). Vowel length and some stress are only approximate, so treat it as a rough guide and trust the stress marks and macrons on the page.

chat.name: simple spoken Classical Latin (active-Latin style; mark long vowels with macrons)

translit.name: Stress guide: CAPITALS mark the stressed syllable, · separates syllables, macrons (ā) mark long vowels

notes.title: How this pack works: reading first, active Latin
body: Your goal is reading real Latin without a dictionary. The fastest route is lots of easy Latin you can understand, so this pack is built like Ørberg's method: texts that explain themselves, grammar introduced a little at a time, and Latin used actively. You say and write simple sentences, and you can hold a simple conversation with Claude.
Ørberg's own books are copyrighted, so the readers here are original. Authentic texts (Caesar, the Vulgate, an adapted Phaedrus fable) appear from Unit 11 on.

Each word gets a **reading card** (Latin sentence → meaning) and a **production card** (English → Latin). Shadowing and reading aloud keep a light oral habit, which research on active methods suggests helps reading.

notes.title: Your Spanish is a superpower
body: Most Latin words have a Spanish descendant that follows regular sound changes: ĕ → ie (terra → tierra), ŏ → ue (porta → puerta), f- → h- (fīlius → hijo), -ct- → -ch- (noctem → noche), cl/pl/fl → ll (pluvia → lluvia), p/t/c between vowels → b/d/g (lupus → lobo).
Words show Spanish and English relatives. Spanish nouns usually come from the Latin **accusative** (noctem → noche, partem → parte), which is a handy way to remember the stem.

notes.title: Classical pronunciation
body: You chose **Classical** (restored) pronunciation, the standard in universities and the active-Latin community: c and g are always hard, v sounds like English w, ae sounds like 'eye', and vowel length matters (mālum 'apple' vs malum 'evil').
Stress falls on the second-to-last syllable when it's long, otherwise on the third-to-last. The stress guide under each word shows it in CAPITALS.

notes.title: Unverified content
body: The Latin was written by Claude and checked against standard grammar, but not yet by a human Latinist, so it is marked unverified. Tap ⚑ Flag error on anything that looks wrong.

scriptLessons.title: Pronunciation 1: vowels, length, stress
scriptLessons.note: Latin vowels are pure, like Spanish ones. A macron (ā) means the vowel is held about twice as long. Length can change meaning.

letters.name: short a / long ā
letters.sound: Short a as in 'idea'; long ā as in 'father'. malum 'evil' vs mālum 'apple'.

letters.name: short e / long ē
letters.sound: Short e as in 'pet'; long ē like Spanish e, held longer.

letters.name: short i / long ī
letters.sound: Short i as in 'sit'; long ī as in 'machine'.

letters.name: short o / long ō
letters.sound: Short o as in British 'pot'; long ō a pure 'o' as in Spanish 'no', held longer.

letters.name: short u / long ū
letters.sound: Short u as in 'put'; long ū as in 'rule'.

letters.name: diphthongs oe, au
letters.sound: oe like 'oy' in 'boy'; au like 'ow' in 'how'.

letters.name: the stress rule
letters.sound: Two syllables: stress the first (RŌ·ma). Longer words: stress the second-to-last syllable if it is long (a·MĪ·cus), otherwise the third-to-last (FĒ·mi·na).

scriptLessons.title: Pronunciation 2: consonants (Classical)
scriptLessons.note: Forget Church and Spanish habits for c, g and v. Everything else is close to Spanish.

letters.name: c is always k
letters.sound: Always hard: Cicerō = KI-ke-rō, centum = KEN-tum. Never Spanish z/s or Italian ch.

letters.name: v is w
letters.sound: Like English w: vīnum = WEE-num; vēnī, vīdī, vīcī = WAY-nee, WEE-dee, WEE-kee.

letters.name: consonantal i
letters.sound: Before a vowel at the start of a word, i is y: iam = yam, Iūlius = YOO-li-us. Some books write it j.

letters.name: qu and ngu
letters.sound: qu = kw (aqua = A-kwa); gu after n = gw (lingua = LIN-gwa).

letters.name: r and s
letters.sound: r is tapped or trilled as in Spanish; s is always hissed, never z (rosa = RO-sa).

letters.name: double consonants
letters.sound: Hold double consonants, as in Italian: puella = pu-EL-la, annus = AN-nus.

letters.name: Greek aspirates
letters.sound: In Greek loanwords: p, t, k with a puff of air. Commonly said as f, t, k.

speaking.en: Introduce yourself in Latin: your name, that you're a student, how you are.
Say where five places are and whether they are big or small.
Describe your family: who is who, and whose son/daughter/brother you are.
Say what you do often, always and never.
Describe a house and garden, saying where things are (in + ablative).
Say who gives what to whom (dative).
Be the teacher: give five classroom commands.
Describe Rome or Baltimore: city, river, people, night.
Tell a doctor what hurts and since when.
Tell what you did yesterday, in order (perfect tense).
Retell the fable of the wolf and the lamb in your own words.
Read Caesar's first sentence aloud, then explain it in simple Latin.
hints: Gallia in trēs partēs dīvīsa est.
